# What a workflow manager does {#sec-overview .unnumbered}

A workflow is a set of steps that hand files to each other: one step cleans the
raw measurements of each station, the next fits a model to each, and a last one
summarizes the fits. A shell script runs such steps one after the other, all of
them, every time. A workflow manager is told instead what each step reads and
writes, and works out the rest: the order in which the steps run, which of them
run at once, where they run, on a laptop, a cluster, or in the cloud, and,
after a change or a failure, which of them run again (@sec-model). Everything
it does follows from what the steps declare, and nothing from what they do
without declaring it.

This document explains the ideas that Nextflow and Snakemake share, under the
names each gives them (@sec-terms), says which to use where, and states the
rules that hold for both; the documents of the tools say how. Its rules use the
[normative language](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-normative) of *Design
Principles*.

|  | [Nextflow](nextflow.qmd) | [Snakemake](snakemake.qmd) |
|------------|-----------------------------|-----------------------------|
| Written in | Its own language, built on Groovy | Python, extended with rules |
| Builds the graph | Forward, from the inputs, through channels | Backward, from the files asked for, by patterns of file names |
| Knows a sample by | A value that travels with its files, such as an ID | The names of its files |
| Keeps files | In a directory per task, from which the results are published | Where the rules say |
| Runs again | With `-resume`, the tasks whose hash changed | On every run, the jobs whose outputs are missing or out of date |
| Ready-made workflows | nf-core: maintained pipelines, mostly for genomics | The Snakemake workflow catalog, and wrappers for common tools |

The two do the same job, on the same machines. Snakemake is the shorter way
from a set of scripts to a workflow: its rules are Python, it thinks like Make,
and its files lie where a reader looks for them. Nextflow is the way to run an
nf-core pipeline, which exists for many standard analyses in genomics and is
tested and released by a community, and the more common choice for workflows
that run in the cloud. Within a project, stay with the manager that its
workflows already use: the ideas carry over, the code does not. For a handful
of steps on one machine, Make is enough; in R, the package targets does the job
inside R.

The principles already state what a workflow manager relies on: every step
declares everything its outputs depend on
([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-declared-inputs)), writes all of its
outputs or none ([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-all-or-nothing)), and runs
in a pinned environment ([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-pin)), and the
whole workflow is tested on a small dataset
([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-end-to-end)). The rules below add what
follows from them for every workflow manager.


# At a glance {#sec-at-a-glance .unnumbered}

Every rule of this document in one line. The number and the title link to the
rule.

::: {.glance}
| No. | Rule | In one line |
|-----|------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------|
| [-@sec-pin-manager] | [](#sec-pin-manager) | Run with an exact version of the manager, and a published workflow at a release. |

# How workflow managers think {#sec-model}

A workflow manager is a program that runs for as long as the workflow does. It
reads the workflow, builds the graph of its jobs, starts each job when its
inputs are ready, and waits. It computes nothing itself.


## Steps, jobs, and the graph {#sec-graph}

A step is a command with declared inputs and outputs, written once, such as
"fit a model to the cleaned data of a station". A job is one run of a step on
one input, such as the fit for station 007: a workflow of three steps over a
hundred stations has some two hundred jobs. The manager connects each job that
writes a file to the jobs that read it, and the jobs with these connections form
a graph without cycles, a DAG, which the manager runs (@fig-graph).

![The graph of a workflow with three stations. Each box is a job, one step run on one input, and each arrow a file that one job writes and the next reads. When `012.csv` changes, only the jobs in gray run again.](figures/graph.svg){#fig-graph}

The graph decides the order, and nothing else does. A job runs as soon as all
of its inputs exist, and jobs that do not depend on each other, such as the fits
of two stations, run at the same time, as far as the cores of the machine or
the jobs allowed on the cluster permit. The order in which the steps are
written does not matter. A file that a step reads without declaring it has no
connection in the graph: the job may run before the file is written, and does
not run again when it changes.


## Two ways to build the graph {#sec-pull-push}

Snakemake builds the graph backward, from the files it is asked for, the
targets. For each target, it finds the step whose output pattern matches the
name, such as `results/fits/{station}.parquet` for
`results/fits/007.parquet`, fills in the pattern to learn which inputs that job
needs, and goes on from those, back to files that exist. This is how Make
works. Nothing runs that no target needs, and file names are what connect the
jobs.

Nextflow builds it forward, from the inputs. The workflow puts the input files
into channels, queues of values, and connects the steps by them: a step takes
values from its input channels, runs a job for each, and sends its outputs into
new channels, which feed the next steps. A value carries the identity of a
sample, such as the code of a station beside its file, and the files have no
names or places that matter until the results are published.

Both describe the same graph, and both suit most workflows. They go wrong in
different places: Snakemake when a name matches the wrong pattern
([](snakemake.qmd#sec-patterns)), Nextflow when the values of two channels meet
in the wrong pairs ([](nextflow.qmd#sec-identity)).


## Only what changed runs again {#sec-rerun}

After a change or a failure, a workflow manager runs again only the jobs that
the change affects, and the jobs after them; it reuses the outputs of all
others. This makes a workflow of many hours cheap to change, and it rests on
one assumption: that the manager sees every change that matters. The two
managers see different things.

Snakemake looks at the outputs on disk. A job runs if one of its outputs is
missing or older than one of its inputs, or if its code, parameters, or
environment differ from those it recorded when it made them
([](snakemake.qmd#sec-triggers)). It checks this on every run, without being
asked. Nextflow keeps a cache: it computes a hash of the inputs, the script, and
the environment of every task, and with `-resume`, it reuses a task whose hash
it finds, together with the outputs left in its work directory
([](nextflow.qmd#sec-resume)). Without `-resume`, it runs everything again.

A change that the manager does not see makes nothing run again, and the old
outputs stay, looking as valid as before
([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-loud)): a file that a script reads from a
path of its own, a parameter that a script reads from the configuration instead
of receiving it from the step, a library updated in an environment that is not
pinned. In the other direction, a file that only looks changed, such as a
copy whose times of modification are new, makes the jobs after it run again for
nothing.


## The manager decides, the executor runs {#sec-executor}

The workflow manager does not run the jobs itself; an executor does: on the
machine of the manager, as Slurm jobs on a cluster, or on a batch service in
the cloud. The workflow stays the same, and only its settings for the place
change, which both managers keep in profiles (@sec-profiles). On a cluster,
every job is a Slurm job of its own, with the resources that its step asks for,
and it gets those and no more ([](../scheduling/slurm.qmd#sec-request)).

The manager runs for as long as the workflow, often for days, and while it is
stopped, no new jobs start. It needs little, so most clusters let it run on a
login node, in a session that survives logging out, such as one of `tmux`;
where they do not, it runs as a long job of its own with one CPU. Started again
after it stopped, it continues where it left off (@sec-rerun).


## Each step brings its environment {#sec-environment}

Each step names its environment, a container image or a Conda environment, and
the manager pulls or creates it and starts the jobs of the step in it. Steps can
so use tools whose dependencies conflict, and the environment becomes part of
what a step declares: both managers run a step again when its environment
changes. Pin every environment
([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-pin)), an image as [](../containers/index.qmd)
describes. On a cluster, both managers run the containers with Apptainer, and
pass on the options of [](../containers/apptainer.qmd#sec-host) only when told
to.


# Same ideas, different names {#sec-terms}

The two managers name the same ideas differently, and some of their words mean
something else in the other: a Snakemake *job* is a Nextflow *task*, and a
Nextflow *job* is the Slurm job that runs a task.

| Idea | Nextflow | Snakemake |
|------------------|------------------------------|------------------------------|
| A step | Process | Rule |
| One run of a step | Task | Job |
| What connects the steps | Channels of values | File names, matched by patterns with wildcards |
| What the workflow makes | The outputs that the entry `workflow` publishes | The targets: the files named on the command line, or the inputs of the first rule, usually `all` |
| The workflow | `main.nf`, with modules | `Snakefile`, with `.smk` files |
| Parameters | `params`, from a `params` block, a configuration, and `--name value` | `config`, from a `configfile` and `--config name=value` |
| Where jobs run | The executor, such as `process.executor = 'slurm'` | The executor, such as `--executor slurm`, from a plugin |
| Settings for one place | A profile in `nextflow.config`, chosen with `-profile` | A profile, a directory with a `config.yaml`, chosen with `--profile` |
| The environment of a step | The directives `container` and `conda` | The directives `container` and `conda`, used with `--sdm` |
| Reuse after a change | With `-resume`, by the hash of each task | On every run, by the outputs on disk and their records |
| The record of a run | `-with-report`, `-with-trace`, and `.nextflow.log` | `--report`, and `.snakemake/log/` |


# Rules {#sec-rules}


## Pin the manager, and the workflow {#sec-pin-manager}

A workflow should state the exact version of the workflow manager it runs with,
and a published workflow, such as an nf-core pipeline, should be run at a
release. The manager is a tool that the results depend on like any other
([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-pin)), and its new versions change how a
workflow runs, not only how fast. With version 26.04, for example, Nextflow
began to parse every workflow in its strict syntax, under which a parameter set
on the command line stays text unless its type is declared: `--save false` then
gives the string `'false'`, which counts as true, and the workflow takes the
other branch without a word.

Pin Nextflow with `NXF_VER`, such as `NXF_VER=26.10.3 nextflow run …`, and
require the version in `manifest.nextflowVersion`
([](nextflow.qmd#sec-config)). Install Snakemake from a lock file of the
workflow, into the environment from which it runs; `min_version` in a Snakefile
states only the oldest version allowed. Run a published workflow with its
release, such as `-r 3.27.0` for an nf-core pipeline, not with whatever its
default branch holds today, and record the release with the results
([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-traceability)).


## Resources in the workflow, the place in a profile {#sec-profiles}

Each step should declare what one of its jobs needs, its CPUs, memory, and time,
and the workflow should leave out where it runs: the executor, the partition and
the account on a cluster, the directories for images and environments. These go
into profiles, one per place, such as `slurm` for the cluster and `local` for a
laptop. The same workflow then runs everywhere, and nothing about one cluster
has to be edited out of it before it runs on another, or in continuous
integration.

A profile `test`, which runs the workflow on a small dataset on any machine, is
then the test of [](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-end-to-end): every nf-core
pipeline has one, run with `-profile test`.


## The workflow wires, the steps compute {#sec-thin}

The workflow should say what runs, on which files, and in which environment,
and leave the computation to the scripts and packages that its steps call. Both
managers accept code inline: Snakemake runs Python in the `run:` block of a
rule, and Nextflow runs Groovy in closures and `exec:` blocks, in the process of
the manager, outside the environment of any step. Science written there can be
neither tested nor run without the workflow, nor reused by the next one. It
belongs in library code
([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-library)), which a step calls through
the command line of the package or a short script. Inline code then only
wires: it builds lists of files, chooses a branch by the configuration, or
renames, and the workflow holds little more than names, patterns, resources, and
environments, which a reader can check at a glance.


## Keep the record of every run {#sec-records}

Every run whose results are kept should keep its record with them: the report
of the manager, the configuration and parameters it ran with, and the commit of
the workflow ([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-traceability)). Nextflow writes
its report with `-with-report` and `-with-trace`, and Snakemake with
`snakemake --report report.html` after the run: which jobs ran, with which
commands and environments, and what they used. The manager knows better than
anyone afterwards what ran, but its logs, `.nextflow.log` and `.snakemake/log/`,
lie hidden in the directory it ran in and do not travel with the results.
